submission.natural_language_explanation: L15/N3642− fires on the token that completes a verbatim re-use of a name already present earlier in the context: the second or later occurrence of an exactly repeated identifier, proper name or mathematical symbol (the 'Data' of a second 'JSONData', the 'asa' of a third 'Vasa', the 'b' of '-b' after '14*b'), and for a multi-token name the peak sits on its final token while its earlier pieces stay near zero. The first occurrence of the same string, an equivalent but differently spelled name, repeated ordinary words or repeated comment prose, common words that merely recur and repeated API calls all stay at baseline, so the unit is keyed to re-referencing an established name rather than to token identity, rarity, position or generic repetition, and the distance between the two mentions barely matters (5-150 tokens tested).

Q:

Python Segmentation Fault?

First off, I didnt even know a memory error / segfault was possible in python. Kudos to learning something new!
I have this database I create
database = DBManager(dbEndpoint,dbUser,dbPass,dbSchema)

And then I try to use it in a thread
def stateTimeThreadStart():
     database.getTable('CLIENTS')

threads = []
threads.append(threading.Thread(name='State Updater', target=stateTimeThreadStart, args=()))
threads[0].start()

The output is 
Segmentation fault: 11

What on earth is going on here? It definetly has something to do with database.getTable('CLIENTS') because when I comment it out the issue does not occur. In addition, I have also tried to pass the database to the thread with no luck. Any ideas?
Thanks!

A:

Segmentation faults in Python can occur due to database connectors. The drivers used to connect to the database are usually coded in a C base, so in case of RAM overload or perhaps other reasons it throws Segmentation Faults.
This is further exacerbated by the fact that you are using multithreading. Most database drivers are known to throw Segmentation Faults if multithreading isn't handled very carefully. Most database driver protocols can not handle multiple threads using the same connection at once.
The rule of thumb is to not share a single connection between threads.

Q:

CMake link directory passing when compiling shared library

Say I have C project with the following structure (simplified):
|- CMakeLists.txt   <- This is root CMake
|- lib
    |- <some source files>
    |- CMakeLists.txt   <- CMake file for building the library
|- demo
    |- <some source files>
    |- CMakeLists.txt   <- CMake for building demo apps
|- extra_lib
    |- <some source files>
    |- CMakeLists.txt   <- CMake for building supplementary library

Now, I want to build my library (living in lib) as a shared library to be used by demo apps from demo directory. 
Additional library, that can not be a part of my library (it is essentially a wrapper for some C++ external library) is also to be compiled as a shared library and then linked to my library.
I have a problem with including dependencies for additional library. In its CMakeLists.txt I've defined link_directories to point location where .so libs are stored and then target_link_libraries to point which should be linked. At the end I did export target.
include_directories(${EXTERNAL_DIR}/include)
link_directories(${EXTERNAL_DIR}/lib)

add_library(extra_lib SHARED extra_lib.cpp)

target_link_libraries(extra_lib
  some_lib
)

export(TARGETS extra_lib FILE extra_lib.cmake)

The point is that when I try to compile lib and link it against extra_lib I get an error that some_lib is not found what I guess means that link_directories is local to the extra_lib.
Now, question is how can I make it propagate together with dependencies? I'd like it to work in the way that adding extra_lib as subdirectory and as a dependency for my lib would automatically add linked directories from extra_lib to the lib linking process.
The linking process would look like:
(some external library) --> extra_lib --> lib --> demo app

A:

First off, the CMake docs state that commands like include_directories and link_directories are rarely necessary. In fact, it is almost always better to use target_include_directories and target_link_libraries instead.
Secondly, the reason your approach fails is because you need to let CMake know about the existence of some_lib. You can do this like so:
add_library(some_lib SHARED IMPORTED)
set_target_properties(some_lib
    PROPERTIES
        IMPORTED_LOCATION ${EXTERNAL_DIR}/lib/libsome_lib.so

The first survey of the northern watershed was commissioned in the spring of 1887, when the provincial assembly finally approved a modest budget for a trigonometric network linking the coastal ports to the interior plateaus. The work fell to a small team of engineers who had spent the previous decade mapping railway corridors, and they brought with them a habit of precision that would shape every later map of the region.

Their instruments were modest: a pair of theodolites, a chain of brass rods calibrated against a standard held in the capital, and a set of astronomical tables that had been corrected by hand for refraction. Field notes from that season describe weeks of fog, ruined observations, and the slow business of reoccupying stations marked only by cairns of stacked slate.

The plateau itself proved harder than expected. Streams that appeared on earlier sketches turned out to be seasonal, and several valleys were found to drain north rather than west, forcing the team to resurvey a corridor they had already crossed twice. Local herders, whose knowledge of the passes was far better than anything in the archives, were hired as guides, and their place names gradually replaced the improvised labels the engineers had used in the first drafts.

By the autumn of 1889 the network had reached the eastern escarpment, and the assembly published a preliminary sheet at one inch to the mile. It was accurate enough to guide the first telegraph survey, though it misplaced a ridge by nearly a mile, an error that was not corrected for another generation.

The second survey, begun in 1912, benefited from photography, from lighter instruments, and from a generation of engineers trained in the new polytechnic institutes. Rather than reoccupying the old stations one by one, the team established a fresh chain of control points along the rivers and tied the earlier work into it. The comparison was unflattering: some angles differed by minutes of arc, and several elevations were wrong by tens of feet. Yet the older observations, made in worse conditions and with heavier gear, held up better than anyone had expected.

In the winter of 1921, Mirabel Okonkwo, who had joined the service as a computer in the years before the war, was given the task of reconciling the two datasets. She spent three winters at the plateau office, checking every reduction and re-deriving the constants from the original field books. Her marginal notes, written in a cramped hand, record a running argument with the earlier surveyors that is by turns patient and exasperated. In the end she kept most of their stations, discarded four, and added a correction table that remained in use until the satellite era.

The map that emerged from this work is still the basis for land disputes in the valley, and copies of it hang in several municipal offices. Visitors often assume it is a modern product, so clean are its contours and so consistent its shading. Only the faint pencil annotations along the margins hint at how much argument, and how many ruined observations, went into drawing them.

In 1954, Mirabel Okonkwo returned to the plateau office to supervise the transfer of the archive to microfilm, and the notes she had written three decades earlier were finally typed up and bound.
